title: Chapter 1: The Gate Opens Twice
content: The ninth passenger steps aboard at 9:41 and the ferry sits a thumb width lower in the water.

Wren counts them from the apron with one hand on the chain. Bride in white, hem gone gray to the shin. Groom with his tie hanging loose. Two groomsmen in matching vests. Two bridesmaids carrying their shoes. Arlen Sample with his bicycle lifted over the rail like a calf. Ida Quill with a cooler she will not set down. Tobe Quill, eleven, told to sit, not sitting.
Nine.
The plate welded to the hull says nine. Elias has said a thousand times that the plate is a promise and the river is a loan.
"Nine," she calls back to the wheelhouse.
"Then bring up the apron."

She brings up the apron. The chain dogs into the notch, the pin goes home, and she leans on it twice to hear it seat. The drum takes the cable with a sound like a spoon dragged along a fence. The ferry walks out from the east ramp into the dark.

The wedding was at four at the Methodist church on Mill Street and the reception after that at the diner. Ruthie Pyle made the cake, and the cake fell on the left side, and Ruthie filled the hole with strawberries and told the room it was meant to look like that. Della Fenn is twenty-two and has wanted this since she was fourteen. Curtis Rudd is twenty-four and has wanted Della since he was fourteen. Denny Rudd, the groom's brother, has been singing since the soup.

They are loud and warm and they smell like beer and hairspray, and Wren does not mind them. A full boat on a Saturday is a good boat. The ferry has run since 1908 and her family has run it since 1975, and a full boat is the only argument this town has ever needed.

The Sable is wide at Mile 9. Wide enough that the far bank is a rumor of lights and a smell of diesel and fried food. Kestrel House sits up on the bluff with every window lit, white and square, like a piece of Columbus that fell off a truck and landed in the trees.

Wren runs the drum and the apron and the book. Elias takes the wheel and the hook. He is seventy-eight and moves like a man who has been doing one thing for fifty-one years, which he has. Short sentences. He calls her girl when he is pleased and Wren when he is not, and she has learned to hear the difference across two hundred feet of water.

The book is under the bench in the wheelhouse, hardbound, green, the color gone to the color of a pond. It starts in 1961 because the one before it burned. Elias wrote the first page in his own hand at nineteen, and he has written every passenger since, name and date, and now she writes half of them too, and their two hands sit on the page together like a man and his shadow.
Tonight she writes the run before they cast off, the way he taught her. Twelve September, two thousand twenty-six. Nine forty-four in the evening. Nine souls.
She likes the old word. Elias says the county likes it too, because a soul is not a passenger and a passenger is not a soul, and the book has always been careful about which one it meant.
Then the names, in the order they came aboard. Della Fenn. Curtis Rudd. Denny Rudd. Porter Vail. Nessa Vail. June Pettit. Arlen Sample. Ida Quill. Tobe Quill.

The night is warm for September. The water is still soft enough to swim, and two boys were in it at the sandbar below the landing at six o'clock, and the katydids are going in the willows like a pump that needs fixing. The river is at the second rung of the ramp. It has been at the second rung since Tuesday.
Tobe Quill comes up the side deck and stands too close to her elbow, which is what eleven-year-olds do.
"Is it deep here?"
"Forty feet."
"All the way down?"
"All the way down."
He thinks about that. "What's at the bottom?"
"Bicycles," she says. "Ask your uncle."

They are two thirds across when the light on the west ramp goes small and yellow behind them, and Elias eases the drum, and the cable hums. Nine forty-six. The bride is dancing with her father at the bow, badly, both of them laughing, and the cooler has been opened, and Denny Rudd is telling the groomsman about a truck.
The sound comes first.

Not a siren. A knock, low and long, like a door closing in a room under the water. Wren has heard it twice in her life, both times in daylight, both times with a warning on the radio and a man from the gate on the telephone saying hold your crossing.
Tonight there is no radio. Tonight the knock comes and the river stands up.

It comes from below and behind, a hump of black water with a skin on it, and it takes the ferry under the stern and lifts. Six feet in ninety seconds. The cable, which was a bar of tension across the whole river, goes soft. The drum spins free with a shriek, the handle whipping, and the ferry drops back and swings, and the whole boat goes sideways into the current like a door blown off a hinge.
Della Fenn screams. So do the bridesmaids. Arlen Sample's bicycle goes over the rail and is gone without a sound.

Elias is forward. He has the hook and he is pushing a cottonwood limb the size of a car off the bow, and he is winning, and then the deck tilts and the limb comes back and he has one hand on the rail, one hand on the hook, and his boots are not on anything.
He does not call out. That is the part she will keep.
The rail is there. His hand is not.
Wren has two seconds of being a girl on a boat. Then she is the ferryman, because there is nobody else on this deck who knows where the brake is.

She takes the drum. The brake is a foot pedal and a lever and she gets both, and the cable comes taut again with a bang that runs up through the deck into her teeth. The ferry is against the downstream piling, grinding, the apron folded up like a Sunday paper. She works the drum by hand, one turn at a time, and the boat comes around, and the east ramp comes at them out of the dark, and she puts the apron down on it hard enough to shear the pin.
Nobody falls in. That is the thing she will be able to say.

She stands at the apron and counts them off out loud. "One. Two. Three." Della, then Curtis, then Denny, then Porter, then Nessa, then June, then Arlen, then Ida with her cooler, because Ida will not let go of the cooler. Then Tobe, and she takes his hand for the last step, and he is shaking so hard he nearly takes her down with him.
Nine. She counts them twice.
"Go up to the diner," she says. "Call from the diner. Tell Ruthie."
"Where's Mr. Aubrey?" Curtis says.
"Go up the bank."

Her voice is level. She hears it and does not recognize it. Della is crying with her shoes in her hand and her hem black to the knee. They go up the ramp in a knot, and the katydids go on with their business, and the river, which was six feet lower four minutes ago, lies flat and wide and innocent as a field.
Up on the road a porch light comes on at the Quill place, then another at the Samples'. Somebody is running. Somebody is already calling Ruthie, who will already know, because Ruthie always knows.
Wren takes the light off its hook. She takes the boat hook too. She walks down the east bank with the beam on the water and calls his name, and the water gives her back nothing but the light.

She finds him forty feet down, against the piling, where the slack cable runs under the surface. His jacket has ballooned and gone pale in the beam. His hand is caught in the cable and his face is in the water.

She was nine years old the last time she went into this river after somebody. It was August, at Mile 11, and the car was upside down in the shallows with the windows down, and her mother was still in the driver's seat with her seatbelt on, and a man in a hat put his hand on Wren's chest and said that is enough now, honey, and she has never once in fifteen years been able to remember his face.
She does not stop this time.

She gets the hand out of the cable. She gets her arms under his and drags him up the gravel, and he is heavier than a man has any right to be, and she is making a sound she has never heard herself make. She lays him flat. She tips his head. She puts the heels of her hands on his chest and counts, thirty, and gives him two breaths, and his chest goes up and does not come down on its own, and there is water at the corner of his mouth, and she wipes it and keeps counting.
His hand is in her hand. She is still counting when he stops.
Ten oh four. She knows because she looks at her watch, and she will always know, the way she knows the plate says nine and the water was at the second rung.
She sits back on the gravel with his head in her lap and his jacket dripping, and the light lies on its side and shines at nothing, and up on the levee road a man is standing in a clean jacket.

He has a clipboard. He has a lanyard that says Basin Authority and a haircut from a city. He has been there for some part of it. He does not come down the bank. He does not kneel. He looks at the two of them the way a man looks at a figure in a column that will not add up.
"Ma'am," he says. "Is that Elias Aubrey?"
"Yes."
He writes nothing. The pen is still clipped to the board.
"Was anyone else in the water?"
"No."
"How many aboard?"
"Nine."
He looks at the ferry, then at the river, which has already begun to go down, the way it always does, six feet up and then six feet back, and the bank is left with a wet line on it like a tide.
"Gate ran a maintenance release at nine forty-seven," he says. "That's all I can tell you tonight."
Wren does not answer him. She is looking at the pen.
Then he asks the question, in the same flat voice, as if it were the next item on a list.
"Was he on the clock?"
highlight: At 9:47 the gate pulses without a siren, nine passengers reach the bank, and Elias does not.
